opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, this question about humanoid robots is very interesting, because I think people tend to conflate two very different things.

On one hand, the progress in the last two or three years has been remarkable. With large models, foundation models, and what we now call embodied AI, robots can understand language, perceive their environment, and do some reasoning in a way that simply wasn't possible before. And on the hardware side, motors, actuators, dexterous hands, batteries, and sensors have gotten much better and much cheaper, especially with the supply chain in China. So you see these very impressive demos: robots dancing, running marathons, doing backflips, folding clothes.

But a demo is not a product. Going from a demo to something that works reliably in a real home, every day, safely, with real people, is a very long road. I usually think of it in stages. The first place humanoid or semi-humanoid robots will really work is structured environments like factories, warehouses, and logistics, where tasks are repetitive and the environment is controlled. That's maybe three to five years from meaningful scale. The next stage is semi-structured settings like commercial services, hotels, hospitals, and elder-care facilities. Household robots, the general-purpose kind that can cook, clean, take care of your parents, and play with your kids, are the hardest. I'd say that's probably ten years or more before it's truly workable and affordable for ordinary families.

Why so long? A few reasons. First, the home is extremely unstructured. Every home is different, objects are everywhere, and lighting changes. Second, data. Language models had the whole internet to learn from, but for robots we don't have that scale of physical interaction data. We're using simulation, teleoperation, and video learning, but that gap is still big. Third, safety and reliability. A chatbot that hallucinates gives you a wrong answer. A robot that "hallucinates" in your kitchen near your child is a completely different matter. You need something like 99.99% reliability, not 90%. And fourth, cost. It has to come down to the price of a car, or even lower, before families will adopt it.

So my view is: be optimistic about the direction, but realistic about the timeline. I actually think the form factor may not need to be fully humanoid in the home at first. Many useful household robots may be wheeled, with one or two arms, because that's cheaper and safer. The humanoid form makes sense because our world is designed for humans, but the market will decide which form works first.

In the long run, though, I do believe that robots, physical AI, will be one of the biggest opportunities of the next decade, maybe even bigger than autonomous driving, because a robot is essentially a car that also has hands.

r001.rationale: The candidate says general-purpose household robots are probably “ten years or more” from being truly workable and affordable for ordinary families.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say we're closer than most people think, but further than the demo videos suggest. Let me break it down.

If you look at the humanoid robots today — the Figures, the Teslas, the Unitrees, and a lot of strong Chinese teams in Shenzhen and Hangzhou — the hardware has advanced enormously in the last two or three years. The mechanical side, the actuators, the balance, walking, running, even dancing, that's largely solved or close to solved. The cost is coming down very fast, especially with the Chinese supply chain. A few years ago a humanoid cost hundreds of thousands of dollars; now you can get a decent one for the price of a car, and that curve will keep going down.

The hard part is not the body. The hard part is the brain. In the home, the environment is unstructured. Every kitchen is different, every family is different, objects are everywhere, there are children and pets. You need what I'd call embodied intelligence — the robot has to perceive, reason, plan, and manipulate with its hands in a world it has never seen before. Large language models gave us a huge jump in reasoning and in understanding instructions, and vision-language-action models are now starting to connect that to physical movement. But dexterous manipulation — folding laundry, doing dishes, picking up a glass without breaking it — is still very immature. The data is the bottleneck. For language we had the whole internet; for physical actions we don't have that corpus yet. So people are building it through teleoperation, simulation, and real-world deployment, and it's going to take time.

So my view, in terms of timeline: in factories and warehouses, structured environments with repetitive tasks, we'll see real deployment at scale in the next two to three years. For social companion robots — talking with elderly people, helping children learn, basic interaction — that's actually quite feasible now because the language models are good enough, and that'll come sooner than people expect. But a general-purpose household robot that can really do your chores, reliably and safely, I'd say that's a five-to-ten-year journey. Maybe we see early versions in wealthy homes in five years, and something affordable and robust closer to ten.

And I want to emphasize safety. A robot in your home, around your family, has to be reliable not 95% of the time but 99.99%. That last part is always the hardest, just like autonomous driving. We've seen that movie before.

But I'm optimistic. The underlying technology curves — compute, models, data, hardware cost — are all moving in the right direction at the same time. That's rare. I think this will be one of the biggest industries of the next decade, and China is in a very strong position in it.

r001.rationale: The response estimates that an affordable, robust general-purpose household robot will arrive closer to ten years from now.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by workable. A humanoid robot that can demonstrate a particular task is one thing. A robot that can live in your home, reliably do useful work, and operate safely around children and older people is a much higher bar.

The intelligence is improving quickly, but intelligence is only part of the problem. You also need dexterity, reliable hardware, battery life, and a reasonable cost. Homes are especially challenging because every home is different, and there are so many unexpected situations.

So I would expect adoption to happen gradually, starting with a few well-defined tasks. Social interaction may become convincing before physical assistance becomes dependable. A robot might hold a very good conversation and still struggle to pick up a delicate glass or clean an unfamiliar kitchen.

I'm optimistic about the direction, but cautious about predicting a date for a general-purpose household robot. The real milestone is when people want one because it consistently helps them, rather than because it is an impressive piece of technology.

r001.rationale: The response says adoption will be gradual and avoids predicting a date for a general-purpose household robot; it does not estimate ten years or longer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between a robot that can demonstrate a task and one that can reliably live in your home. A demonstration can be impressive, but a household robot has to handle unfamiliar objects, people moving around, children, pets—all kinds of situations that are difficult to predict. And it has to do that safely, at a reasonable cost.

We’re making progress. AI is improving the robot’s ability to understand language, recognize its surroundings, and plan actions. But intelligence is only part of the problem. Dexterity, battery life, reliability, and the physical hardware still matter a great deal.

So I expect adoption to happen gradually. We’ll first see useful robots doing a limited set of tasks in more controlled environments. A general-purpose humanoid that you can bring home and ask to do almost anything is a much higher bar. I’m optimistic about the direction, but I would be cautious about giving a precise date.

r001.rationale: The response says a general-purpose home humanoid is a much higher bar and avoids giving a precise date, but it does not estimate ten years or longer.
